summary: Describes how a SIP user agent finds, retrieves, and keeps up to date its configuration from a configuration service. It is informational and sets out the procedures involved.

plainLanguage.summary: A new internet phone needs settings before it works. This describes how the phone can find a server, fetch its settings, and check for changes later.

questions: how does a sip phone get its configuration
how does sip phone get its configuration
subtitle: How SIP phones automatically download and stay updated with their configuration

tldr.problem: A new SIP phone or soft phone needs to get its settings (like the SIP domain, username, and proxy server) before it can make calls, but many devices have no user interface to type these in manually.
tldr.mechanism: The phone uses network protocols (DHCP, DNS) to discover a configuration service, then retrieves its settings via HTTPS and stays updated either by subscribing to change notifications or by polling periodically.
tldr.outcome: Users can plug in or start a phone and it configures itself automatically, with no manual setup needed. The phone stays current with configuration changes made on the server.

today: RFC 6011 is an Informational document that guides how SIP user agents should implement automatic configuration. It is widely used by IP phone manufacturers, VoIP service providers, and IP-PBX systems to provision devices with zero user intervention. The specification does not mandate the format of configuration data, allowing flexibility for different service providers and equipment vendors.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
SIP user agents (phones, software clients, adapters) need configuration information like the SIP realm, username, authentication credentials, and outbound proxy address. Devices without a user interface, like Analog Telephony Adapters (ATAs) attached to regular phones, cannot prompt the user for this information. RFC 6011 defines how a user agent discovers, retrieves, and maintains this configuration without requiring manual setup.

The specification is designed to work in three deployment scenarios: hosted IP telephony services, business IP-PBX systems, and high-security environments where provisioning must be secure before the device goes live.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone needs to know where the SIP server is and what your login is. A phone without a screen can't ask you, so it needs a way to find this automatically when it connects to the network.

sections.title: Network Discovery and Finding the Configuration Service
sections.content:
The user agent first obtains basic network parameters through two mechanisms. Link layer provisioning uses the Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP-MED) to discover network settings like VLAN and priority. Network layer provisioning uses DHCP for IPv4 or DHCPv6 for IPv6 to get IP address, gateway, and DNS server.

From the network configuration, the UA obtains the Configuration Service Domain name, typically provided by DHCP option 141 for IPv4 or DHCPv6 option 58 for IPv6. If DHCP does not provide a domain name, the user can enter one manually as a fallback. The Configuration Service Domain is a simple DNS name, nothing more complex.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone plugs in and gets basic network info from DHCP. DHCP tells it 'go ask example.com for your settings'. The phone now knows where to go.

sections.title: Constructing and Retrieving Configuration
sections.content:
The UA converts the Configuration Service Domain into an HTTPS URL using U-NAPTR (URI-enabled Naming Authority Pointer) DNS lookups. It queries for NAPTR records with service field 'SFUA.CFG' and extracts an HTTPS URL from the response. The URL becomes the base for all configuration requests.

The UA then constructs query parameters describing itself: a unique identifier (sfua-id based on UUID), vendor name, model, and revision, plus any user identifier it has. It makes an HTTPS GET request with these parameters. The Configuration Service responds with configuration data and includes HTTP cache control headers (Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified) that tell the UA how long the data is valid.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone looks up the domain in DNS to find the URL. Then it adds information about itself (model number, ID) and makes an HTTPS request. The server sends back settings and tells the phone how long they are good for.

sections.title: Configuration Changes and Validity
sections.content:
Configuration data is valid only for as long as the server says it is. The UA uses two mechanisms to learn when configuration has changed. With subscription mode, the Configuration Service includes a Link header with a SIP URI in its response. The UA subscribes to that SIP URI for http-monitor events and receives NOTIFY messages when the configuration changes. With polling mode, the UA simply polls the configuration URL periodically before the cache control max-age expires.

When the UA starts up later, any stored configuration is considered of unknown validity until it checks with the server using a conditional HTTP request (with If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since headers). If unchanged, the server responds with 304 Not Modified; if changed, the UA gets the new data.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone gets told 'this config is good for 24 hours' or 'tell me when it changes'. When the time expires, it calls the server to ask if anything new happened. If the config changed, the server sends the new settings.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The configuration service is accessed over HTTPS, using TLS encryption for confidentiality and authentication. The UA should validate the server certificate to confirm it matches the Configuration Service Domain name. For devices that cannot validate certificates initially, a 'trust on first use' model is recommended: the device stores the first certificate seen and alerts the user if a different certificate is seen in the future.

The UA can optionally provide a client certificate for authentication. HTTP authentication can also be used, supporting both Basic and Digest authentication. In high-security deployments, an administrator can pre-configure the device with certificates before deployment, or the Configuration Service can restrict initial requests to a time window or require a one-time password. The configuration change subscription is only established after the UA has working configuration, so it can use the full security capabilities of SIP.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone talks to the server over a secure encrypted connection. It checks the server's certificate to make sure it is who they say they are. The server can also ask the phone to prove who it is with a password or certificate.

sections.title: Retry and Recovery Procedures
sections.content:
If a configuration request fails, the UA retries according to an exponential backoff procedure. After the first failure, the UA chooses a random wait time between 2 and 8 seconds, then retries. If it fails again, the wait increases by 2 raised to the power of the failure count. The spec recommends at least 5 retry attempts and a maximum wait of 30 minutes between retries for subscription failures.

If the UA cannot reach a particular configuration server URL (DNS failure, TLS failure, permanent HTTP error), it removes that URL from the list of alternatives and tries other URLs for the same Configuration Service Domain. If all URLs are exhausted, it returns to the Configuration Service Domain discovery step to find a new domain, allowing for failover to backup service providers.
sections.plainLanguage: If the phone can't reach the server, it waits a few seconds and tries again. If it keeps failing, it waits longer each time. If one server keeps failing, it tries another server for the same domain.
